title: Weekly pilot metrics and guardrail calibration with Selene AI
summary: Weekly POC sync to review latest quality evals, discuss a small regression in hallucination rate on the clinical-notes prompt set, tune guardrails and scoring thresholds, and agree next steps: run expanded regression tests, share revised prompt set spreadsheet, and schedule a focused SE-led benchmarking session against their 1k eval suite.
next_steps: Ethan to run expanded regression sweep (1k prompts) and deliver results by 2025-08-25
Maya to send revised prompt spreadsheet and scoring rubric by 2025-08-22
Priya to schedule SE benchmarking slot (90 mins) for week of 2025-08-26
Selene team to prepare 3 example failure cases and share logs by 2025-08-24
action_items: Ethan - run 1k prompt regression with kv-cache disabled and tag anomalies - due 2025-08-25
Maya - update prompt set CSV with suggested fallbacks and share link - due 2025-08-22
Priya - book 90-min benchmarking window and invite infra contact - due 2025-08-23
Ava (Selene) - export and share 20 hallucination examples with trace logs - due 2025-08-24
questions: Can we reproducibly trigger the hallucination with a fixed seed?
Is the regression dataset covering the same corpus distribution as production?
Do we prefer stricter guardrail rejects or more conservative paraphrase rewrites?
transcript:
Meeting header: 2025-08-21 15:00 UTC / duration 48m / recording by Fireflies
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Ethan Rodriguez (Redwood SE), Priya Kapoor (CSM), Liam Park (Selene CTO), Sofia Martinez (ML Eng), Noah Ibrahim (Product Manager), Ava Liu (Data Scientist)

[00:00] Maya: Hey everyone uh thanks for joining, we'll kick off, quick agenda - quality review, regression notes from Selene, prompt set changes, and next steps.
[00:22] Liam: Thanks Maya, quick note we only have 45 minutes so maybe prioritize the hallucination regression, that's most urgent.
[00:30] Maya: Totally, we'll jump there first. Ethan do you want to run through the eval numbers?
[00:36] Ethan: Yeah sure. So on the latest run - we saw overall accuracy up 2% on the summarization set, embeddings stable, but there's a spike in hallucination rate specifically on the clinical-notes prompt bucket - from 3.1% to 7.8% week over week.
[00:55] Sofia: Right and those clinical notes are the primary critical path for us because downstream QA flags are costly.
[01:02] Ethan: Understood. Initial triage - differences look correlated with a prompt template change where conditional examples were reduced, also we noticed an ngram tokenization mismatch when the sequence exceeded 1k tokens causing different attention patterns.
[01:20] Noah: Sorry can you repeat the tokenization mismatch bit?
[01:22] Ethan: Yeah, so our tokenizer split on a couple of clinical abbreviations differently than your preprocessing variant; that changed the positional indexing and possibly the KV cache alignment in long sequences — leading to rare weird completions.
[01:35] Ava: We did roll a small change to strip dots from abbreviations two weeks ago, that could be it.
[01:40] Liam: So the regression might be on our side with preproc. Are we confident Redwood's runtime could have introduced anything?
[01:47] Ethan: We can't rule out runtime interactions. We saw a handful of cases where prefix caching produced slightly different logits when using batching vs single-infer. I suspect a combination of preproc + batching alignment differences.
[02:05] Maya: Good, that gives us a clear hypothesis. Let's talk guardrails — currently you have guardrail policy set to warn on hallucination but not block; would you consider stricter behavior for clinical-notes?
[02:18] Liam: We would but we worry about turning off returns entirely - many times the model provides useful content even if partial. Maybe rewrite/restrict versus block.
[02:26] Sofia: For downstream workflows, a conservative paraphrase-and-flag flow is better than silent block.
[02:32] Ethan: We can implement a two-tier guardrail: 1) reject when hallucination confidence > .9, 2) otherwise return sanitized paraphrase + flag metadata. That keeps availability but reduces risk.
[02:46] Noah: How do we compute "hallucination confidence"? Is that from the model or from a scoring heuristic?
[02:52] Ethan: It's a heuristic ensemble: token-level anomaly score + semantic similarity to a reference index + a small calibration model we run post-hoc. We can share the rubric.
[03:05] Maya: We'll upload the scoring rubric as a spreadsheet. Priya will attach it to the follow-up.
[03:12] Priya: Yep will do.
[03:14] Sofia: Also curious about latency impact if we add the paraphrase step or calibration model inline.
[03:20] Ethan: Good point — paraphrase step adds ~120-250ms on our hosted path; calibration model adds 80-150ms depending on concurrency. With batching we can amortize but it costs tokens and cost.
[03:33] Liam: Cost matters but so does SLA; if paraphrase keeps business continuity we might accept a small latency bump.
[03:40] Maya: We can present two configs: conservative (paraphrase + flag) and strict (reject). We'll quantify token/cost delta.
[03:48] Ava: Related - we saw a small increase in average token lengths on failing cases, could be probe prompts from product tests. Not sure if that's correlated.
[03:55] Ethan: We'll run a filtered analysis on token distributions. Ethan -> action.
[03:58] Noah: okay. On prompts - we had suggested five prompt templates, we updated three — can you confirm which ones you used in the last eval?
[04:08] Ethan: We used the current CSV you shared dated 2025-08-12, but we also applied our standard normalizer; there may be subtle differences.
[04:16] Sofia: That's the mismatch then. We should sync prompt normalization rules.
[04:19] Maya: Let's add a normalization spec row in the prompt CSV so both sides apply same preproc.
[04:24] Liam: Sounds good.
[04:26] [06:10] Ethan: Quick detour — on regression detection we recommend adding a rolling A/B with 10% of traffic pinned to previous prompt+preproc so regressions are caught early.
[06:20] Liam: Can Redwood do canary routing at that granularity?
[06:24] Ethan: Yes - we can pin requests by user or session id and route to previous model variant; can also compare token-level diffs via trace.
[06:33] Noah: That would be helpful.
[06:36] Maya: We'll propose a rollout plan in the follow-up doc.
[06:42] [08:00] Maya: Okay let's look at the sample failure cases you shared - Ava, can you walk us through one or two?
[08:06] Ava: Sure. Example 1 - prompt is clinical note: "Patient presents w/ hx of DMII, bg 210, rx metformin." Model hallucinated that the patient had 'recent onset ketoacidosis' — which is false in the chart.
[08:22] Ethan: Looking at that, the hallucination likely came from the model over-generalizing the high glucose value + ambiguous phrasing.
[08:30] Sofia: The model is inferring diagnosis, which our guardrails should prevent.
[08:34] Ethan: We can tweak the prompt to include an explicit instruction: "Do not infer diagnoses; only summarize stated diagnoses." Also add a rejection signal if the model inserts new diagnoses not present in input.
[08:46] Maya: We'll add that to the prompt set as a hard constraint in the conservative config.
[08:51] Noah: Any quick wins for reducing hallucination without impacting generation quality?
[08:55] Ethan: Token-level stopwords and bracketed evidence copying help; also augmenting with a small retrieval check against the record can reduce incorrect claims. Retrieval adds latency but is high precision.
[09:07] Liam: We can accept retrieval for clinical notes.
[09:10] Ethan: Great. We'll prototype a lightweight retrieval step.
[09:15] [12:20] Maya: On metrics, we've been tracking: hallucination_rate, ROUGE-variant, semantic-similarity (cosine), and downstream QA flags. Any other useful metrics?
[12:28] Ava: Precision on factual claims would help; maybe claim-level F1.
[12:32] Ethan: We'll add claim-F1 to the rubric.
[12:35] Maya: Also we'll add a 'regression delta' column comparing week over week.
[12:40] [15:00] Ethan: Small note - we observed KV cache alignment issues when batch sizes > 8 for 1k+ sequences. For safety, you might limit batching for very long sequences or use per-request inference for those.
[15:12] Sofia: What's the throughput hit if we do that?
[15:15] Ethan: Depends on concurrency; expect a 15-30% throughput reduction for those long requests if we disable batching. But per-token cost goes up.
[15:24] Liam: For clinical-critical flows we prefer correctness over throughput.
[15:28] Maya: Good call — we'll propose a separate SLA class for long clinical sequences.
[15:34] [21:50] Priya: Quick commercial note - if you want dedicated capacity for these long sequences, Dedicated pools give stable latency; we can size based on your 99th percentile. I can loop in sales ops.
[21:59] Liam: Put a placeholder, we'll evaluate.
[22:03] [26:00] Maya: Back to prompt CSV - action item: add normalization spec, add guardrail flags per prompt, and a fallback rewrite template. We'll attach an example.
[26:12] Ava: Can you also add examples of both acceptable and unacceptable outputs for each prompt? That helps calibrate the scoring model.
[26:19] Ethan: Yes we'll include accept/reject examples and explain feature signals we look at.
[26:24] [30:00] Noah: On the SE benchmarking slot, we want a dry run where you run our 1k suite and walk through the failures live so we can iterate on prompts.
[30:08] Ethan: Sounds good — we'll allocate a dedicated runner and stream results.
[30:12] Priya: I'll coordinate times, expecting 90 minutes.
[30:17] Maya: Final quick risk question from compliance - does Redwood keep raw prompts in logs?
[30:22] Ethan: By default we persist minimal trace info; for Private customers you can opt for no raw prompt retention and token-level redaction. We'll share the compliance doc.
[30:33] Liam: We'll need that doc for our security review next week.
[30:37] [35:00] Maya: Okay let's recap decisions: hypothesis is preproc + batching alignment; mitigation plan = normalized prompt CSV + two-tier guardrail + targeted regression sweep + lightweight retrieval for clinical notes; next meeting plan = SE benchmarking session.
[35:18] Noah: That matches our expectations.
[35:22] Maya: Any blockers?
[35:25] Liam: Not from us; just need the docs and scheduled benchmarking.
[35:30] Maya: Great. We'll follow up with the spreadsheet and a calendar invite.
[35:35] Priya: I'll send invites and attach rubric.
[35:40] Ethan: I'll start the regression runs after this call.
[35:44] Ava: We'll gather the 20 exemplar failures and push to the shared folder.
[35:50] Maya: Thanks everyone, we'll close out.
[36:00] [End of recording]
file_notes: Transcription has some minor ASR errors for technical terms (kv-cache, tokenization); speakers used both first names and roles, we preserved original labels. Links referenced: will include prompt CSV, scoring rubric, compliance doc in follow-up email.
